usage: Formal word for staying overnight somewhere; you'll see it on booking sites and signs.
비 = fee/cost; the price you pay for the night.
하다 verb form; more formal than just 자다 (to sleep).
Standard way to count a trip's length; read as '일박 이일'.
examples: 숙박은 어디서 하세요?
Where are you staying?
Common question when chatting about a trip; 어디서 = where (at).
숙박비가 생각보다 비싸네요.
The lodging is pricier than I expected.
-네요 adds a mild 'oh' reaction; natural in conversation.
주말이라 숙박이 거의 다 찼어요.
It's the weekend so the rooms are almost all booked.
다 찼어요 = all filled up; 거의 = almost.
nuance: 숙박 is the umbrella term that covers any kind of overnight stay, from a hotel to a guesthouse. It feels official and shows up on reservation apps, receipts, and signs, whereas in casual speech people often just say where they're sleeping (호텔에서 자요).
mistakes: Don't confuse 숙박 (the act of staying) with 숙소 (the place itself).
숙박하다 is for staying the night, not for a daytime visit — use 가다/들르다 for that.

usage: Budget lodging with shared spaces; very popular with young travelers in Korea.
Common shortened form among 20-30s; 게스트하우스 → 게하.
A shared room with bunk beds, the cheapest option at a guesthouse.
Read '일인실'; a private room if you don't want a shared dorm.
examples: 저는 여행할 때 보통 게스트하우스에 묵어요.
When I travel I usually stay at a guesthouse.
묵다 = to stay/lodge, slightly more formal than 자다.
게하에서 친구를 많이 사귀었어요.
I made a lot of friends at the guesthouse.
사귀다 = to make (friends); 게하 is the casual short form.
이 게스트하우스는 조식이 무료예요.
This guesthouse has free breakfast.
조식 = breakfast (lodging context); 무료 = free of charge.
nuance: 게스트하우스 are a staple of cheap travel in Korea, especially in Jeju and Busan, and they're known as places to meet other travelers at shared dinners or parties. Young people almost always shorten it to 게하 in speech and texts, so recognizing the slang is essential.
mistakes: 게스트하우스 is written as one long loanword — don't split it as '게스트 하우스' in writing.
Don't assume every room is shared; many offer 1인실 or 2인실 private rooms too.

usage: A private house or unit rented out, usually in the countryside or near the coast.
A higher-end 펜션 with a private pool; trendy for group getaways.
Most 펜션 have a 바비큐 area — a big reason groups book them.
로 marks the manner; 펜션 are ideal 단체로 (for a group).
examples: 친구들이랑 펜션 빌려서 놀러 가기로 했어요.
We decided to rent a pension with friends and go hang out.
빌리다 = to rent; -기로 했어요 = decided to.
이 펜션은 바다 바로 앞이라 전망이 좋아요.
This pension is right by the sea so the view is great.
바로 앞 = right in front; 전망 = view.
펜션에서 바비큐 해 먹는 게 제일 좋아요.
Eating barbecue at the pension is the best part.
해 먹다 = to cook and eat; -는 게 = the act of.
nuance: A 펜션 in Korea is not a retirement payment (that's 연금) — it's a private vacation house you rent, usually for a group of friends or a family. They're the default choice for a weekend getaway because you get a whole space, a kitchen, and a barbecue area, unlike a hotel room.
mistakes: 펜션 is a false friend — it never means a retirement pension (use 연금 for that).
펜션 usually means renting the whole unit, so don't expect hotel-style services like daily cleaning.

usage: A large complex with lodging plus pools, spas, restaurants, often near beaches or ski slopes.
A common facility inside a summer 리조트.
What you book a winter 리조트 for; 장 = grounds/field.
The extra facilities a 리조트 advertises (pool, gym, sauna).
examples: 겨울에 스키 타러 리조트에 갔어요.
I went to a resort to ski in winter.
스키 타다 = to ski; -러 가다 = go in order to.
리조트 안에 워터파크가 있어서 애들이 좋아해요.
There's a water park inside the resort so the kids love it.
안에 = inside; -아서 = because/so.
리조트는 비싸지만 부대시설이 잘 돼 있어요.
Resorts are expensive but the amenities are well set up.
잘 돼 있다 = to be well equipped; -지만 = but.
nuance: 리조트 implies a self-contained vacation complex, a step up from a plain hotel, where you can spend the whole stay without leaving — think ski resorts in Gangwon or beach resorts in Jeju. People use it when the facilities themselves (water park, spa, slopes) are the point of the trip.
mistakes: A 리조트 is bigger and more facility-focused than a 호텔, so don't use the two interchangeably.
Don't confuse 리조트 (resort complex) with 콘도 / 콘도미니엄, which is a membership-based unit you book inside many resorts.

english: homestay, B&B in a private home
usage: Staying in a room of someone's house, often rural or seaside.
집 = house; the place where you do a 민박.
The person whose home it is; 주인 아주머니/아저씨 cooks and chats.
민박 are most common 시골에서 (in the countryside).
examples: 바닷가 근처 민박에서 하룻밤 잤어요.
We slept one night at a homestay near the beach.
하룻밤 = one night; 근처 = nearby.
민박집 주인 아주머니가 아침을 차려 주셨어요.
The homestay host (auntie) made us breakfast.
차려 주다 = to set out (a meal) for someone; honorific 주셨어요.
호텔보다 민박이 더 정겨워요.
A homestay feels warmer/homier than a hotel.
정겹다 = warm-hearted, homey; -보다 더 = more than.
nuance: 민박 is staying in a spare room of a local family's home, the most old-school and personal lodging type, common in fishing villages and the countryside. Unlike a 펜션 where you have the place to yourself, a 민박 means sharing space with the host family, which many travelers find charming and inexpensive.
mistakes: Don't confuse 민박 (a room in someone's home) with 펜션 (a separate rental unit) or 게스트하우스 (a budget shared-room lodging).
Watch the spelling: it's 민박 (박, 'stay/night'), not 민방 — the final consonant is ㄱ, not ㅇ.

usage: Leaving and settling up at a hotel/lodging; the loanword is standard.
The arrival counterpart; you'll always hear these two together.
하다 verb form used at the front desk.
The key thing to ask: 체크아웃이 몇 시예요? (What time is check-out?)
examples: 체크아웃이 몇 시예요?
What time is check-out?
Essential front-desk question; 몇 시 = what time.
체크아웃하고 짐을 맡길 수 있어요?
Can I leave my luggage after checking out?
맡기다 = to leave/entrust; very common request.
늦게 체크아웃하면 추가 요금이 있어요.
If you check out late there's an extra fee.
추가 요금 = extra charge; -면 = if.
nuance: 체크아웃 is the universal loanword used at every hotel, guesthouse, and 펜션 in Korea, always paired with 체크인. Knowing to ask 체크아웃이 몇 시예요? matters because late checkout often triggers an 추가 요금, and you can usually ask to store luggage (짐 보관) afterward.
mistakes: Don't use the native word 나가다 (to leave) when you mean the formal hotel process — say 체크아웃.
Late checkout is 레이트 체크아웃 or 늦은 체크아웃; it's usually not free, so confirm first.

usage: Busy travel periods like summer vacation and holidays when prices spike.
극 = extreme; the very busiest stretch (e.g., late July to mid-August).
오르다 = to rise; what happens to lodging in 성수기.
꽉 차다 = packed full; rooms sell out in 성수기.
examples: 성수기에는 펜션 값이 두 배예요.
In peak season pension prices double.
두 배 = double; 값 = price.
성수기라 비행기표 구하기가 힘들어요.
It's peak season so plane tickets are hard to get.
구하다 = to obtain; -기가 힘들다 = is hard to do.
성수기를 피해서 가는 게 좋아요.
It's better to go avoiding peak season.
피하다 = to avoid; -는 게 좋다 = it's good to.
nuance: 성수기 covers the high-demand travel windows — summer (여름휴가), Chuseok, Seollal, and ski season — when lodging and flights cost far more and sell out fast. Residents plan around it constantly, often saying they want to 성수기를 피하다 (avoid peak season) to save money and crowds.
mistakes: 성수기 is the opposite of 비수기 (off-season) — don't mix them up.
성수기 refers to demand periods, not the weather; a sunny day isn't 성수기.

usage: Quiet travel periods when prices drop and places are empty.
비수기 is when you get the best 할인 on lodging.
Describes how a tourist spot feels 비수기 (in the off-season).
examples: 비수기에 가면 훨씬 싸요.
If you go in the off-season it's much cheaper.
훨씬 = much (more); 싸다 = cheap.
비수기라 사람이 별로 없어서 좋았어요.
It was off-season so there weren't many people, which was nice.
별로 없다 = not many; -아서 = so.
비수기에 여행하는 게 가성비가 좋아요.
Traveling in the off-season is great value.
가성비 = cost-effectiveness, popular slang.
nuance: 비수기 is the off-season — weekdays, late autumn, or deep winter outside ski areas — when lodging slashes prices and attractions are calm. Budget-minded 20-30s love it for the 가성비, since you get the same place for much less and skip the crowds of 성수기.
mistakes: 비수기 is the exact opposite of 성수기; learn them as a pair.
Don't read 비 here as 'rain' — 비수기 has nothing to do with rainy weather.

english: day trip (there and back same day)
usage: Going and returning the same day with no overnight stay.
로 marks the manner: 당일치기로 다녀오다 (do it as a day trip).
The verb that pairs with 당일치기.
무박 2일 = an overnight-less trip; an extreme day trip.
examples: 부산은 서울에서 당일치기로 다녀올 수 있어요.
You can do Busan as a day trip from Seoul.
다녀오다 = go and return; -ㄹ 수 있다 = can.
당일치기라 짐을 가볍게 쌌어요.
It's a day trip so I packed light.
가볍게 = lightly; 짐을 싸다 = to pack.
당일치기 여행이라 좀 빡빡했어요.
It was a day trip so it was a bit tight (rushed).
빡빡하다 = tight/packed (slang-ish, common).
nuance: 당일치기 means a same-day round trip with no overnight — hugely practical in Korea thanks to the KTX, so a Seoul resident can do Busan or Gangneung 당일치기. It pairs naturally with 다녀오다, and the schedule tends to be 빡빡하다 (tight) since you cram everything into one day.
mistakes: 당일치기 implies returning the same day — if you sleep over, it's 1박 2일 instead.
Use 다녀오다 (go and come back), not just 가다, since the whole point is the round trip.

usage: City lights or scenery seen at night; a major sightseeing draw.
명소 = noted spot; e.g., Namsan Tower, the Han River.
The most common compliment about a place at night.
Where you go for the best 야경 (e.g., 남산 전망대).
examples: 남산에서 보는 서울 야경이 진짜 예뻐요.
The Seoul night view from Namsan is really pretty.
에서 보는 = seen from; 진짜 = really.
야경 보러 한강에 갈래요?
Want to go to the Han River to see the night view?
-러 가다 = go to do; -ㄹ래요? = casual invitation.
이 카페는 야경 맛집이에요.
This cafe has an amazing night view.
야경 맛집 = slang: a place 'great for' night views, by analogy to food 맛집.
nuance: 야경 is the night view — glittering city lights from a 전망대, bridge, or rooftop — and it's a core part of how Koreans enjoy cities after dark. Young people stretch the foodie word 맛집 into 야경 맛집 to mean 'a spot with a killer night view,' which you'll see all over social media.
mistakes: 야경 is specifically the scene at night; daytime scenery is just 경치 or 전망.
Don't confuse 야경 (night view) with 야간 (nighttime, the time period).

usage: The sun coming up; a big deal especially on New Year's Day.
Pure-Korean synonym for 일출; 해돋이 보러 가다 is very common.
Places like 정동진, 호미곶 known for 일출.
Watching the first sunrise of the year is a popular tradition.
examples: 새해 첫날 일출 보러 동해에 갔어요.
We went to the East Sea to see the New Year's sunrise.
첫날 = first day; 동해 = East Sea.
일출을 보려고 새벽 5시에 일어났어요.
I got up at 5 a.m. to watch the sunrise.
-려고 = in order to; 새벽 = dawn.
구름이 껴서 일출을 못 봤어요.
It was cloudy so we couldn't see the sunrise.
구름이 끼다 = to get cloudy; 못 봤어요 = couldn't see.
nuance: 일출 (or the native 해돋이) is sunrise, and watching it carries real cultural weight — crowds head to the east coast to see the 새해 일출 (first sunrise of the year) and make wishes. It pairs with early-morning effort words like 새벽 and 일어나다, since catching it means getting up before dawn.
mistakes: 일출 is the opposite of 일몰 (sunset) — keep the pair straight.
Both 일출 and 해돋이 mean sunrise; the native 해돋이 sounds warmer and is just as common in speech.

usage: The sun going down; prized at west-coast spots.
The colored sky at 일몰; 노을이 지다 = the glow spreads.
What you check before heading to a viewpoint.
Literary synonym you'll see in captions and signs.
examples: 서해는 일몰이 아름답기로 유명해요.
The West Sea is famous for beautiful sunsets.
-기로 유명하다 = famous for; 서해 = West Sea.
일몰 시간에 맞춰서 바닷가에 도착했어요.
We arrived at the beach right at sunset time.
에 맞춰서 = timed to; 도착하다 = to arrive.
노을이 너무 예뻐서 사진을 계속 찍었어요.
The sunset glow was so pretty I kept taking photos.
노을 = the glow; 계속 = continuously.
nuance: 일몰 is sunset, the counterpart to 일출, and Korea's west coast (서해) is the classic place to watch it sink into the sea. In everyday speech people often talk about the 노을 (the colorful afterglow) rather than the technical 일몰, especially when sharing photos of a pretty evening sky.
mistakes: 일몰 is sunset, not sunrise — its pair is 일출.
일몰 names the event (sun setting); 노을 names the colored sky — use 노을 when you mean the pretty glow.
